extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, judges, and law students studying infringement doctrine
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing infringement and validity issues arising from combination patents, substitution/equivalents (mechanical and chemical), and the effect of useless or non‑novel parts. Focuses on when use of part(s) or equivalents constitutes infringement and when multi-part claims are severable or void.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement by use of a material part of a combination
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a patent is for an invention consisting of several parts, the imitation or pirating of any part of the invention is an infringement of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a patent claims a combination of parts, a user of the entire combination is clearly infringing; but even if only a material part of that combination is taken and used by another, that can be an actionable infringement. Example: a machine of three parts where one part is 'very useful' — copying that material part (even if substituting other modes for the less useful parts) may sustain an action for infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial-identity requirement for combination claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent for a combination is for the union of all the parts arranged and combined as stated in the specification; the use of only some parts is not the same combination unless what is used is 'substantially the same thing.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether use of less than the whole combination is infringement is a fact question for the jury: courts ask whether what the defendant used was 'substantially the same' as the patented combination. If the defendant's combination 'substantially differs' in any of its parts or arrangement, it is not the same combination. (Prouty v. Ruggles discussion.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical equivalents doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: If the defendant has employed a mechanical equivalent as a substitute for some material element of the plaintiff's combination, that will be an infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanical equivalents are substitutions that a person skilled in the art could adopt from his knowledge of the art (e.g., a spring instead of a weight to produce downward pressure). If the substitution requires no inventive step for a skilled mechanic, it is a mechanical equivalent and constitutes infringement. The doctrine is not confined to strictly technical mechanical nomenclature but embraces substitutions judged by construction to accomplish the same end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between mechanical equivalents and independent inventions producing same result
rubrics_metrics.description: Two things may be equivalent as producing the same result but not be mechanical equivalents if they operate by different mechanisms and require invention to adopt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: hauling water by rope and bringing it by an invented pump both produce the same result, but the pump is not a mechanical equivalent of the rope because it introduces different powers and forces and required invention. Only substitutions that a skilled practitioner could make without further invention are mechanical equivalents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of any one of several distinct improvements may infringe (but validity requires novelty of each)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a patent claims several distinct improvements or things (not standing as a single combination), the use of any one of them will be an infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically, for such multi-improvement patents the whole patent could be void if any one claimed improvement lacked novelty because the grant's consideration was the novelty of all the things together; however, statutes and later cases modify this rule (see severability below). Whether a patent 'stands upon the combination' or on distinct inventions affects whether copying one improvement infringes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory severability of overbroad patents (validity as to material and substantial parts)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent shall be deemed good and valid for so much of the invention as shall be truly and bona fide the invention of the patentee, if it is a material and substantial part of the thing patented and is definitely distinguishable from the other parts which the patentee had no right to claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statutory rule salvages patents that were accidentally or mistakenly made too broad, allowing the valid, material, and distinguishable portions to remain enforceable — provided the overbreadth was not wilful or intended to defraud the public. The earlier doctrine that lack of novelty in any part vitiated the whole still applies where claims were knowingly made too broad to deceive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of lack of utility of one claimed part (false suggestion doctrine)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a thing claimed as essential turns out to be useless and was known by the patentee to be useless when the specification was enrolled (a false suggestion of usefulness), the patent is voidable/void for misrepresentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a part is subsequently discovered to be useless (but not known to be so at enrollment), that does not necessarily vitiate the patent. A patent for an entire machine that is useful on the whole will be valid even if parts are useless, so long as there was no false suggestion of utility at the time of grant. Courts distinguish between known-in-fact useless elements (which can void the patent) and those only later found impractical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chemical (composition) equivalents and claim scope
rubrics_metrics.description: To substitute in place of some element in a composition a mere known equivalent is an infringement, because the patentee is understood in law to embrace known equivalents unless he expressly confines his claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In composition patents, a patentee may limit his claim to specific ingredients and thereby exclude equivalents; if he expressly disclaims or excludes an ingredient (e.g., 'without the addition of ... sulphuret of antimony'), he is estopped from later asserting that ingredient is covered. Courts examine the specification language and what a skilled person would understand the patentee to have intended to cover. Factual inquiry (e.g., whether the defendant's product contains the excluded substance) controls enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Express disclaimers/control public notice principle
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee who expressly excludes particular equivalents or ingredients in the claim is taken to have waived them, and cannot assert those excluded alternatives as covered by the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One object of the patent specification is to inform the public what may be safely done without infringement during the patent term. If the patentee's claim language plainly excludes an equivalent, that exclusion governs even if it was based on mistake; patent law provides mechanisms to correct mistakes, but until corrected the record controls. (Byam v. Farr discussion.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Product claims can be infringed irrespective of the process used
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the specification amounts to a claim for the product (article) itself, the patent may be infringed by any one using the article regardless of the manner in which it was made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although sometimes obiter, courts have held that a product claim covers the article per se: if the patent covers the product, manufacture or use of that product by others infringes even if they used a different manufacturing process. This contrasts with situations where only a process is claimed.
